summary: Specifies Bidirectional Forwarding Detection, a protocol to detect faults in the bidirectional path between two forwarding engines, with potentially very low latency. It works independently of media, data protocols and routing protocols. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Two neighbors keep saying I am here to each other very quickly, so they notice almost right away if one goes silent.

questions: how fast is bfd failure detection
subtitle: A lightweight hello protocol that lets two neighbouring systems notice a broken path in a fraction of a second.

tldr.problem: Routing protocol Hellos detect failures no faster than about a second, some media give no hardware failure signal, and each protocol invents its own detection method.
tldr.mechanism: Two systems exchange small BFD Control packets at negotiated intervals over each path, and declare the session Down when enough packets in a row stop arriving. A three-way handshake brings sessions up and down.
tldr.outcome: BFD gives one media-independent, protocol-independent liveness mechanism with a wide range of detection times. RFC 5880 is a Proposed Standard that has since been updated by several later RFCs.

facts.label: Auth types
facts.value: 5 (Simple Password, Keyed and Meticulous Keyed MD5 and SHA1)

today: RFC 5880 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It has been updated by RFC 7419, RFC 7880, RFC 8562 and RFC 9747, so those should be read alongside it.

sections.title: Why Faster Failure Detection
sections.content:
Networks need to notice quickly when a neighbour stops being reachable, so that traffic can move to another path. Some media help: SONET raises alarms in hardware. Others, such as Ethernet, do not, and some media miss certain failures, for example a failing interface or forwarding engine component.

Where hardware gives no help, networks rely on the slow Hello mechanisms of routing protocols. The RFC says the detection times of existing protocols are no better than a second, which is far too long for some applications and represents a lot of lost data at gigabit rates. Routing Hellos also only detect a failure between two routing protocol engines, and they are no help when no routing protocol is in use.

The goal of Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) is low-overhead, short-duration detection of failures in the path between adjacent forwarding engines, including interfaces, data links and, to the extent possible, the forwarding engines themselves. A second goal is a single mechanism for liveness detection over any media, at any protocol layer, so that methods do not proliferate.
sections.eli5: Imagine two kids with tin-can phones. If one stops answering, the other wants to know right away, not after a whole minute of waiting. BFD is a very quick way of checking that the other side is still there.

sections.title: Design and Operating Modes
sections.content:
BFD is designed to detect failures in communication with a forwarding plane next hop. It is intended to be implemented in the forwarding engine where forwarding and control are separated, which decouples it from the fate of the routing protocol engine and makes it useful with graceful restart mechanisms. It always runs in unicast, point-to-point mode, on top of any data protocol, and can monitor direct links, virtual circuits, tunnels, MPLS LSPs, multihop routed paths and unidirectional links, as long as there is some return path. A separate session exists for each path and data protocol in use.

There is no discovery mechanism: the application that needs BFD decides the addresses to use. For example, an OSPF implementation may ask for a session to a neighbour it found with the OSPF Hello protocol.

BFD has two modes and one add-on function:

  • Asynchronous mode is the primary mode. Systems send BFD Control packets periodically, and if a number of them in a row do not arrive, the session is declared down.
  • Demand mode assumes a system has some other way to confirm connectivity. It can ask the peer to stop sending periodic packets, and verify connectivity only when it wants to.
  • The Echo function sends packets that the other system loops back through its forwarding path. It works with either mode and allows the rate of Control packets to be reduced or, in Demand mode, eliminated.

Pure Asynchronous mode needs half as many packets as the Echo function for a given detection time. Echo tests only the remote forwarding path, which may reduce round-trip jitter. Demand mode suits systems with a very large number of sessions, but its detection times depend on the implementation, and it may not be used when the path round-trip time is greater than the desired detection time.
sections.eli5: There are three ways to check on a friend. You can both shout hello every second, you can stay quiet and only ask when you wonder, or you can throw a ball and see if it bounces back.

sections.title: The BFD Control Packet
sections.content:
A BFD Control packet has a mandatory section and an optional Authentication Section. The encapsulation (what it is carried in) is outside this RFC and is covered by application documents. The mandatory section starts with Vers (version 1 is defined here), Diag, Sta and six flag bits: P (Poll), F (Final), C (Control Plane Independent), A (Authentication Present), D (Demand) and M (Multipoint, which MUST be zero).

Next come Detect Mult and Length, then two discriminators, My Discriminator and Your Discriminator, which identify the session at each end. Three interval fields follow, all in microseconds: Desired Min TX Interval, Required Min RX Interval and Required Min Echo RX Interval. A required receive interval of zero means the sender wants no periodic Control packets. A zero echo interval means it cannot loop back Echo packets.

The Sta field carries the sender's view of the session: 0 AdminDown, 1 Down, 2 Init, 3 Up. The Diag field gives the reason for the last state change, such as Control Detection Time Expired, Echo Function Failed or Administratively Down.

Echo packets have no defined format. Their payload is a local matter, since only the sender processes it, but it must allow the looped-back packet to be matched to its session, and some form of authentication SHOULD be included because Echo packets may be spoofed.
sections.eli5: Each hello message is like a little card. It says who is writing, what shape they think the friendship is in, and how often they would like to get cards back.

sections.title: The Session State Machine
sections.content:
A session normally moves through three states, giving a three-way handshake for both setup and teardown, so both systems know about every state change. A fourth state, AdminDown, holds a session down on purpose. Each system sends its state in the Sta field, and the received state plus the local state drives the machine.

  • Down: the session is down or just created. It advances to Init if the peer reports Down, and to Up if the peer reports Init.
  • Init: the peer is communicating but does not yet realise the local system wants the session up. It advances to Up when a packet signals Init or Up, and falls back to Down if the Detection Time expires.
  • Up: the session is established and connectivity is working. It drops to Down if the peer signals Down or the Detection Time expires.
  • AdminDown: the session is held down by an administrator, which makes the remote system go Down and stay there. It says nothing about whether the forwarding path is available.

Packets are matched to sessions with the discriminators. Each system picks a nonzero discriminator that is unique among its sessions. Once the peer echoes it back in Your Discriminator, all further packets are demultiplexed on that field alone, so the source address or the receiving interface can change without breaking the session. How the very first packets (where Your Discriminator is zero) are matched is application dependent.

A system takes an Active or Passive role at start-up. An Active system sends Control packets regardless; a Passive one MUST NOT send until it has received a packet and learned the peer's discriminator. At least one side MUST be Active.
sections.eli5: It is like a handshake with three steps: I wave, you wave back, and then we both know we see each other. If either of us stops waving for too long, we both go back to not being sure.

sections.title: Timers, Polling and Detection
sections.content:
Each side says how fast it would like to send and how fast it can receive. The sender MUST NOT transmit faster than the larger of its own Desired Min TX Interval and the peer's Required Min RX Interval, so the slower side sets the rate. Each direction is independent. Transmission is jittered by up to 25% per packet to avoid self-synchronisation, and while a session is not Up the desired transmit interval MUST be at least one second (1,000,000 microseconds).

The Detection Time is not sent in the packet. The receiver calculates it. In Asynchronous mode it is the received Detect Mult multiplied by the remote system's agreed transmit interval; roughly, Detect Mult is the number of packets in a row that must be missed. If no valid Control packet arrives within that time while the session is Init or Up, the session goes Down with diagnostic 1.

A Poll Sequence is how a system makes sure its peer has noticed a change or verifies connectivity in Demand mode. The sender sets the Poll bit; the receiver answers at once with a packet that has the Final bit set; the sequence ends when the Final arrives. A packet MUST NOT have both bits set. Changing the desired transmit or required receive interval requires a Poll Sequence, and when the transmit interval is increased the old interval is kept until the sequence finishes, so the peer's Detection Time is updated first.

In Demand mode a system sets the D bit and the peer stops sending periodic packets. The bit MUST NOT be set unless both sides see the session as Up. The Echo function may only be used once the session is Up and the peer advertised a nonzero Required Min Echo RX Interval. If enough Echo packets go missing, the session goes Down with diagnostic 2.
sections.eli5: Both friends agree how often to say hello, and the slower friend sets the pace. If you miss a few hellos in a row, you decide something is wrong. If you want to change the pace, you ask first and wait for a thumbs up.

sections.title: Authentication Options
sections.content:
The optional Authentication Section carries what the receiver needs to judge whether a Control packet is genuine. Choosing the type and exchanging keys happens outside the protocol. Implementations that support authentication MUST support both SHA1 types; the others are optional.

The five types are Simple Password (type 1), Keyed MD5 (2), Meticulous Keyed MD5 (3), Keyed SHA1 (4) and Meticulous Keyed SHA1 (5).

  • Simple Password sends a password of 1 to 16 bytes with a key ID in every packet. It is the weakest form.
  • Keyed MD5 and Keyed SHA1 put a digest of the whole packet in the packet, calculated with a secret key that is never sent. A sequence number guards against replay and is incremented only occasionally. The Auth Len is 24 for MD5 and 28 for SHA1.
  • Meticulous variants increment the sequence number on every packet, and the receiver accepts only a sequence number strictly greater than the last one, within a window of 3 times Detect Mult.

The RFC says the use of MD5-based authentication is strongly discouraged and is documented only for compatibility with existing implementations.

Authentication should not be switchable by incoming packets alone. A simple approach is to allow the authentication state to change at most once without some form of intervention.
sections.eli5: It is a secret handshake on every card. The better versions change the handshake a little each time, so a sneaky copycat cannot just replay an old one.

sections.title: Operational Notes and IANA
sections.content:
BFD is likely to be a critical part of network infrastructure, so disruption must be avoided. Anything that blocks BFD packets, such as a firewall, will make it fail. Policers, shapers and priority queues can disturb it when the Detection Time is close to the packet scheduling rate. Across multiple hops a congestion control mechanism MUST be implemented, and one SHOULD be used even on a single hop, because systems with many sessions or very short intervals can become CPU-bound. The ways to reduce load are the Min RX and Min TX interval fields, and any increase in them lengthens the Detection Time.

The RFC gives a sizing example: a detection time of 50 milliseconds, from a transmit interval of 16.7 milliseconds and a detect multiplier of 3, produces 60 packets per second. At around 100 bytes per packet that is about 48 kilobits per second in each direction.

IANA keeps two registries created by this document, BFD Diagnostic Codes (initial values 0 to 8, with 9 to 31 unassigned) and BFD Authentication Types (0 to 5, with 6 to 255 unassigned). New entries go through Expert Review.
sections.eli5: Quick hellos are cheap, but if a whole crowd shouts hello too often it gets noisy. So BFD asks everyone to back off when things get crowded.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because BFD can be tied to the stability of routing, an attack on a session can be serious: a link can be falsely declared down or falsely declared up, and either way the effect is denial of service. An attacker in full control of the link can drop only the BFD packets, or forward only the BFD packets, and BFD cannot prevent that.

Against weaker attackers the RFC names two defences. The first is the Generalized TTL Security Mechanism (RFC 5082): on a single directly connected link, the TTL or Hop Count MUST be set to the maximum on transmit and checked to equal the maximum on receipt. The second is the Authentication Section, which SHOULD be used across multiple hops or an insecure tunnel such as GRE.

Simple Password is only as secure as the password and should be considered only where packets cannot be intercepted. The keyed types are stronger since keys cannot be read from packets, with the meticulous types stronger still; SHA1 is believed to have stronger properties than MD5. They use a secret suffix construction rather than HMAC, which the RFC believes appropriate for BFD. Randomising the local discriminator can further reduce replay attacks.

Echo packets are defined only by their sender, so cryptographic authentication does not prove the other system is alive: an attacker could loop them back and make the link look up. A suitable interval for Control packets mitigates this.
sections.eli5: A bad guy could pretend your friend is still there, or pretend they are gone. BFD uses secret handshakes and checks that hello cards came from nearby to make that harder.

fields.name: Vers
fields.desc: Protocol version; this document defines version 1.

fields.name: Diag
fields.desc: Reason for the last change in session state.

fields.name: Sta
fields.desc: Sender's session state: AdminDown, Down, Init or Up.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the packet in bytes.

fields.name: Your Discriminator
fields.desc: Discriminator received from the peer, or zero if unknown.

fields.name: Desired Min TX Interval
fields.desc: Fastest interval the sender wants to transmit at, in microseconds.

fields.name: Required Min RX Interval
fields.desc: Fastest interval the sender can receive at, in microseconds.

fields.name: Required Min Echo RX Interval
fields.desc: Fastest Echo receive interval in microseconds; zero means no Echo support.

transitions.label: peer reports Down, or Detection Time expires

items.label: No Diagnostic
items.desc: Initial value of the local diagnostic.

items.label: Control Detection Time Expired
items.desc: No valid Control packet within the Detection Time.

items.label: Echo Function Failed
items.desc: Too many Echo packets went missing.

items.label: Neighbor Signaled Session Down
items.desc: The peer reported Down or AdminDown.

items.label: Forwarding Plane Reset
items.desc: The local forwarding plane was reset.

items.label: Path Down
items.desc: Outside signalling said the underlying path failed.

items.label: Concatenated Path Down
items.desc: Forward failure of a concatenated path.

items.label: Administratively Down
items.desc: Session held down by an administrator.

items.label: Reverse Concatenated Path Down
items.desc: Reverse failure of a concatenated path.
